subChunks.title: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK
subChunks.hookHtml: What happens if the power fails halfway through an XP transfer? Without transactions, one account loses XP and the other never gains it. Transactions prevent that.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The problem

Consider transferring 100 XP from Dorian to Alice. This requires two UPDATE statements. If the system crashes between them, the database is in an inconsistent state — XP was subtracted from Dorian but never added to Alice.

The solution: ACID transactions

BEGIN;                               -- start transaction
UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp - 100 WHERE id = 4;  -- Dorian
UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 100 WHERE id = 1;  -- Alice
COMMIT;                              -- make permanent

If anything goes wrong between BEGIN and COMMIT, you can undo everything:

BEGIN;
UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp - 100 WHERE id = 4;
-- Oops! Dorian doesn't have 100 XP. Undo everything:
ROLLBACK;

ACID properties

  • Atomicity — either all statements in the transaction succeed, or none of them do
  • Consistency — the database moves from one valid state to another valid state
  • Isolation — concurrent transactions do not see each other's uncommitted changes
  • Durability — once committed, changes survive crashes

Autocommit

Most SQL engines run in autocommit mode by default — each statement is its own transaction. You only need explicit BEGIN/COMMIT when you want multiple statements to be atomic together.

SAVEPOINT

BEGIN;
SAVEPOINT sp1;
DELETE FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice';
-- Only Novices look wrong, keep the rest:
ROLLBACK TO sp1;
-- The DELETE to Novices is reversed; other changes survive
COMMIT;

storyBeats.text: The power flickers as two ledger entries are being written simultaneously. When the candles relight, one entry is complete — the other is gone.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: A transaction is a promise: all of these changes happen, or none of them happen. BEGIN starts the promise. COMMIT seals it. ROLLBACK breaks it — undoing everything back to the BEGIN. Without transactions, crashes leave the archive in impossible states.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 XP transfer analysis

Write the transaction that safely transfers 200 XP from Alice (id=1) to Bjorn (id=2). Include a check after each UPDATE (as a comment) describing what you would verify before COMMITting.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
BEGIN;

UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp - 200 WHERE id = 1;  -- Alice loses 200 XP
-- Verify: SELECT xp FROM apprentices WHERE id = 1; -- should show 1000 (was 1200)

UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 200 WHERE id = 2;  -- Bjorn gains 200 XP
-- Verify: SELECT xp FROM apprentices WHERE id = 2; -- should show 2600 (was 2400)

-- Both look correct:
COMMIT;

-- If either step produced wrong results:
-- ROLLBACK; -- would undo both UPDATEs
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Write a transaction that: (1) promotes all 'Novice' apprentices with xp >= 50 to 'Apprentice', (2) awards them 100 bonus XP, (3) commits only if the total number of Apprentices after the transaction is greater than 2 (describe this as a comment — you cannot branch in SQL without stored procedures).
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what ACID means in plain language using the XP transfer example. Why does Atomicity matter?

questions.prompt: What does ROLLBACK do inside an open transaction?
options: Undoes all changes made since the BEGIN
questions.answer: Undoes all changes made since the BEGIN
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK reverses all changes made within the current transaction back to the state at BEGIN (or the most recent SAVEPOINT if one was set).

questions.prompt: Why wrap an XP transfer (debit one account, credit another) in a single transaction?
options: To ensure either both changes commit or neither does — preventing a state where XP is lost if a crash occurs between the two UPDATEs
Because two UPDATE statements cannot run sequentially without a transaction
To lock both rows so no other user can read them
Transactions are required for any UPDATE in a multi-user database
questions.answer: To ensure either both changes commit or neither does — preventing a state where XP is lost if a crash occurs between the two UPDATEs
questions.explanation: Atomicity guarantees the all-or-nothing property. Without it, a crash after the debit but before the credit leaves the database with XP simply destroyed.

questions.prompt: What does SAVEPOINT sp1 allow you to do?
options: Roll back to that point without rolling back the entire transaction
Commit only the changes before that point
Create a checkpoint that survives a ROLLBACK of the entire transaction
questions.answer: Roll back to that point without rolling back the entire transaction
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK TO sp1 undoes changes after the savepoint but keeps changes before it. The transaction remains open — you can continue making changes or commit/rollback the rest.

questions.prompt: Most SQL engines default to autocommit. What does this mean for safety?
options: Each statement is automatically committed as soon as it completes — a mistake cannot be rolled back unless explicitly wrapped in BEGIN/ROLLBACK
All statements are automatically rolled back if an error occurs
Autocommit prevents any concurrent access to the table
questions.answer: Each statement is automatically committed as soon as it completes — a mistake cannot be rolled back unless explicitly wrapped in BEGIN/ROLLBACK
questions.explanation: In autocommit mode, every statement is its own transaction that commits immediately. To get rollback protection, explicitly wrap statements in BEGIN...COMMIT. Destructive statements (DELETE, UPDATE without WHERE) should always be wrapped.
